blocks.text: Have you ever wondered why some chemical reactions release heat while others absorb it? The secret lies in the energy changes during the breaking and forming of chemical bonds.

blocks.markdown: In chemistry, understanding energy changes is crucial to predicting how reactions occur. One key concept is enthalpy change ($\Delta H$), which represents the heat change at constant pressure. This can be calculated using bond energies.

blocks.title: Enthalpy Change
blocks.text: Enthalpy change ($\Delta H$) is the heat absorbed or released during a chemical reaction at constant pressure.

blocks.markdown:
To calculate the enthalpy change for a reaction, we use the bond energies of the reactants and products. The formula is: 
\[ \Delta H = \text{Bonds broken} - \text{Bonds formed} \]

blocks.title: Calculating Enthalpy Change
blocks.prompt: Calculate the enthalpy change for the reaction: \[ \text{H}_2 + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{HCl} \] given the bond energies: \( \text{H-H} = 436 \text{ kJ/mol}, \text{Cl-Cl} = 242 \text{ kJ/mol}, \text{H-Cl} = 431 \text{ kJ/mol} \).

steps.text: Calculate the total energy of bonds broken: \( \text{H-H} + \text{Cl-Cl} = 436 + 242 = 678 \text{ kJ/mol} \).
Calculate the total energy of bonds formed: \( 2 \times \text{H-Cl} = 2 \times 431 = 862 \text{ kJ/mol} \).
Use the formula \( \Delta H = \text{Bonds broken} - \text{Bonds formed} = 678 - 862 = -184 \text{ kJ/mol} \).

blocks.answer: The enthalpy change for the reaction is \(-184 \text{ kJ/mol}\).

blocks.markdown: A negative enthalpy change indicates an exothermic reaction, where heat is released. Conversely, a positive enthalpy change indicates an endothermic reaction, where heat is absorbed.

blocks.title: Exam Tip
blocks.text: Always double-check your bond energy values and ensure you multiply by the correct number of bonds formed or broken.
